seasons.review_body: Belascoaran, PI is one of the more quietly assured crime shows Netflix Mexico has produced: three feature-length episodes, each adapted from a different Paco Ignacio Taibo II novel, set in 1970s Mexico City with a visual palette that commits fully to the era. Luis Gerardo Mendez plays Hector Belascoaran with the off-balance charm of a man who has no idea what he is doing but keeps going anyway - which is precisely the joke and the point. The show blends detective procedural with deadpan comedy in proportions that critics found effective. Rotten Tomatoes registered 88 percent (2 critics), with Decider calling it stylish and fast-moving. IMDb audience scores confirmed broad approval at 7.3. The three-episode format, each case self-contained and feature-length, gives the show an anthology quality that suits the source material.

# Belascoaran Pi S01E01: "Days in Combat" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

The live show says the name first. Héctor Shayne is introduced as Belascoarán Shayne, and the hour turns identity into performance from the opening frame. A man who has already lost an old life has to explain his new one in front of lights, hosts, and a city that keeps producing dead women and unanswered questions. The neat detective fantasy gets dirt on its shoes fast. "Days in Combat" works because it treats investigation as exposure. To chase the strangler, **Héctor Belascoarán Shayne** has to become visible, and visibility is exactly what the killer understands.

## The Detective Is Born on Television

The episode's smartest first move is refusing to make Héctor's private detective origin feel private. His reinvention arrives through a live-show frame, with the name "Belascoarán Shayne" spoken before the man has fully settled into it. That matters. This detective story does not begin in a shadowy office with a client and a cigarette. It begins under public pressure, with a contestant explaining that crimes get ignored and many remain unsolved.

That framing gives the hour a useful contradiction. Héctor is trying to become serious while the format around him keeps threatening to make him ridiculous. The early line about him becoming a private detective after losing his old life sets up a man who is partly self-invented and partly cornered. He arrives unfinished. He is building the role while already standing inside danger.

The TV segments also give the writing a brisk, abrasive rhythm. Dialogue piles up around the contest structure, with quick exchanges and repeated on-air cues. The pace fits the premise. Héctor is being tested before he has earned authority. When he declares that he will smoke out the strangler stalking Mexico City, the bravado has a crack in it. That crack is the hook. He is chasing the case because the city, the show, and the killer have pushed him into becoming the bait.

## A Plumber, an Office, and the Joke That Pays Rent

The office setup with **Gómez Letrás** is the kind of eccentric detail that could have become cute wallpaper. Instead, it gives the episode a grounded comic hinge. Gómez confirms he is independent, then trades office setup with rules. In a weaker pilot, that beat would decorate the detective's world. Here, it sharpens the sense that Héctor's new profession is being assembled out of scraps, favors, and negotiated space.

That matters because the case is already too large for him. A strangler is stalking Mexico City. A live host announces a killer at large. Héctor is talking big, but his infrastructure is comically fragile. The gap between mission and machinery is the joke, and it lands. He wants to confront a citywide threat while still working out the practical terms of having a place to work.

The episode gets mileage from that imbalance. Héctor's detective identity is improvised, not glamorous. The plumber beat turns the office from genre icon into a bargaining table, and that choice helps the hour stay human. The danger has scale, but the life around it has invoices, rules, and awkward arrangements. Noir works better here because the hero's myth keeps bumping into rent.

## The Killer Wants the Stage

**Cerevro** enters the hour less as a hidden presence than as a force trying to shape the narrative around himself. He wants to be connected to the ongoing killings, and he calls or frames Héctor for involvement. That is a sharper engine than a simple cat-and-mouse chase. The killer is not only evading detection. He wants the detective pulled into the performance.

This is where the TV framing starts to look less like a gimmick and more like a trap. Héctor uses the televised contest structure to pursue leads, but the same structure gives Cerevro oxygen. The host's declaration that "he'll return" and the announcement of a killer at large create a public stage where investigation and spectacle contaminate each other. The episode understands the ugliness of that bargain. To smoke out the strangler, Héctor has to make noise. The noise helps the hunt, but it also feeds the thing being hunted.

The misspelled name and the "lonely tree on a hill" riddle plant useful unease without over-explaining the pilot's menace. They suggest a killer who wants authorship, a signature, a puzzle that proves he is more than a police file. The risk is theatrical villainy. Some of the contest pressure is more compelling than the riddle-box menace around it. Still, the central idea lands: Cerevro's power comes from his ability to make the city look at him through Héctor.

## Paniagua Turns Procedure Into Pressure

**Officer Paniagua** gives the pilot its most useful institutional friction. His contradiction is clean: he wants Héctor to stop playing pretend and accept that the cases are already solved, yet he threatens jail while later becoming involved enough that Héctor is forced into negotiation and proof arrangements. That is good character mechanics. Paniagua represents a system that wants closure more than inquiry.

The episode uses him to press on the central wound mentioned early by the contestant: crimes get ignored, many remain unsolved. If the official position is that the cases are already handled, then Héctor's amateur persistence becomes irritating by design. He is chasing a killer and challenging the comfort of a solved-file story.

The late negotiation, culminating in Héctor handing over proof and facing a warning of extortion, brings that tension into harder territory. The hour began with performance, then ends closer to leverage. That shift is one of the pilot's stronger structural moves. It takes the playful weirdness of the live-show setup and drags it toward paperwork, threats, and evidence. The detective fantasy starts in public embarrassment. It ends with proof changing hands under pressure.

The weakness is pacing. Long silence pockets later in the hour follow the dialogue-heavy contest material. The darker momentum is welcome, but the shift is noticeable enough to feel like a gear change instead of a seamless tightening. The hour has the right destination. It does not always hide the machinery of getting there.

## The Girl With the Ponytail Brings the Case Home

The girl with the ponytail arrives with the episode's clearest emotional wound: her mother was brutally murdered, and the murderer was never found. That beat is essential because it pulls the case away from clever framing and back to grief. The citywide strangler story could become abstract in the television setup, especially when the killer's riddles and Héctor's public persona take over. Her backstory gives the hour a body, a family, and a past that has not closed.

The episode is careful to leave her connection open. Who she is, and how her mother's murder connects to the strangler or stranglers, remains planted for later. That uncertainty works because it expands the pilot's moral field. Héctor's chase is about beating Cerevro at his own game, but it is also about facing the cost of cases dismissed, mishandled, or left to rot.

This is where Héctor's new life gains weight. Losing his old life made him a detective, but other people's losses test whether that identity means anything. The girl with the ponytail is a reminder that unsolved crime is not an interesting puzzle to the people left behind. It is daily weather.

## The Verdict

"Days in Combat" is a sturdy, oddball pilot with a strong central idea: Héctor can hunt the strangler only by stepping into the same public machinery that the killer wants to exploit. The live-show frame gives the hour personality, Gómez Letrás keeps the detective myth nicely scuffed, and Paniagua turns official certainty into an obstacle with teeth. The episode is less smooth when it shifts from rapid contest banter into darker late-hour silence, and Cerevro's riddle energy needs careful handling before it curdles into decorative menace. Still, the pilot earns its hook. It places Héctor between performance and proof, then makes that gap the story's engine. For the season, it plants clean open loops around Cerevro, the girl with the ponytail, and Héctor's uneasy bargain with visibility.

episode_reviews.title: No Happy Ending
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale case puts Belascoaran directly in the police's crosshairs when a corpse appears in his office. It is the most tightly wound of the three episodes and lands the series' running theme - that the system will punish anyone who actually does the work the system claims to want done.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The discovery of the planted body, which reframes everything Belascoaran thought he understood about who is actually in danger.
